n: John opens the story of the Last Supper with its theme: knowing his hour had come to leave the world and return to the Father, Jesus loved his own to the very end — to the uttermost.

f.w: he loved them unto the end
f.g: The Greek can mean both “to the end of his life” and “completely, to the fullest.”

n: During the evening meal, the devil has already planted in Judas’s heart the plan to betray Jesus.

f.g: Better “during supper,” as the meal continues in verse 26.

f.w: put into the heart of Judas

n: Jesus acts from full awareness of who he is: the Father has given him all things; he came from God and is returning to God. His service flows from that secure identity.

f.w: the Father had given all things into his hands

n: He gets up from the meal, takes off his outer robe, and ties a towel around his waist — dressing as the lowest household servant.

f.g: girded = tied around the waist, like a servant’s apron.

n: He pours water into a basin and begins washing and drying the disciples’ dusty feet — a menial task usually left to servants.

f.w: began to wash the disciples' feet
f.g: In the latter days the Lord restored the washing of feet as an ordinance for the School of the Prophets.

n: When Jesus reaches Peter, Peter is shocked: “Lord, are you going to wash my feet?”

f.g: In Greek, “you” and “my” sit side by side for emphasis: “You — my feet?”

n: Jesus tells him he won’t understand now, but he will later.
Peter flatly refuses. Jesus answers that unless Peter lets him wash him, Peter can have no part with him. Accepting Christ’s cleansing service is essential.

f.w: thou hast no part with me

n: Impulsive Peter swings the other way: then wash my hands and head too!

f.g: Typical Peter — all or nothing, wholehearted but not yet understanding.

n: Jesus explains that one who has bathed only needs his feet washed; they are clean — except one. The JST adds that this was a custom under the law, and Jesus did it to fulfill the law.

f.g: A guest bathed at home and needed only his feet washed after walking to the meal.

f.w: ye are clean, but not all

n: He said “not all” because he knew who would betray him.
Having finished, Jesus puts his robe back on, returns to the table, and asks if they understand what he has done.

f.w: Know ye what I have done to you?
f.g: A teaching question inviting them to reflect.

n: They rightly call him Teacher and Lord — and he truly is.

f.g: Master = teacher (rabbi); Lord = one with authority.

n: If their Lord and Teacher washes their feet, they ought to serve one another in the same humble way.
He has given them an example to follow — leadership through lowly service.

f.w: I have given you an example

n: A servant isn’t greater than his master, nor a messenger greater than the one who sent him. If Jesus serves, no disciple is too important to serve.

f.w: The servant is not greater than his lord

n: Knowing this isn’t enough; joy comes from doing it.

f.w: happy are ye if ye do them
f.g: happy = blessed.

n: Jesus excludes one: he knows whom he chose, but scripture must be fulfilled — someone who shared his bread has turned against him.

f.w: lifted up his heel against me
f.g: To show someone the heel was an insulting gesture of contempt or betrayal.

n: He tells them in advance so that when it happens, their faith will be strengthened rather than shattered.

f.g: Again the Greek egō eimi, “I am.”

n: Whoever receives the messengers Jesus sends receives him, and whoever receives him receives the Father. Despite the betrayal, the apostles’ mission stands.

f.w: He that receiveth whomsoever I send receiveth me

n: Deeply troubled, Jesus declares solemnly that one of the Twelve will betray him.
The disciples look at one another, baffled about whom he means.

f.g: doubting = uncertain, at a loss.

n: Reclining next to Jesus is “the disciple whom Jesus loved,” traditionally understood to be John himself, the Gospel’s author.

f.g: Guests reclined on their left side on couches, so the one to Jesus’s right could lean back against his chest.

n: Peter signals to him to ask Jesus who it is.

f.g: beckoned = signaled with a gesture or nod.

n: Leaning back against Jesus, the beloved disciple quietly asks, “Lord, who is it?”

f.g: The closeness of the image suggests intimate friendship.

n: Jesus says it’s the one to whom he gives a piece of bread dipped in the dish — then hands it to Judas. Offering such a morsel was a gesture of honor and friendship, a final appeal.

f.g: sop = a piece of bread dipped in sauce.

n: After the bread, Satan enters Judas. Jesus tells him, “What you are doing, do quickly.” Judas has made his choice.
No one else at the table understands what Jesus meant.

f.w: no man at the table knew
f.g: Even after the sign, the disciples failed to grasp it.

n: Since Judas held the money bag, some thought Jesus was sending him to buy supplies for the feast or give to the poor.

f.g: Giving to the poor was customary on Passover night.

n: Judas takes the bread and leaves at once. John adds four haunting words: “and it was night” — darkness outside and in.
Once Judas is gone, Jesus announces that the Son of Man is now glorified, and God is glorified in him. The path to the cross is now set.

f.w: Now is the Son of man glorified

n: And God will glorify the Son in himself, and do it soon — through the Resurrection and Ascension.

f.g: straightway = immediately, at once.

n: Tenderly calling them “little children,” Jesus says he will be with them only a short while; they cannot come where he is going.

f.g: The only place in the Gospels Jesus uses this affectionate term.

n: He gives a new commandment: love one another as he has loved them. The command to love was old; the new standard is Christ’s own self-giving love.
This love will be the identifying mark of his disciples before the whole world.

f.w: By this shall all men know that ye are my disciples

n: Peter, still stuck on Jesus leaving, asks where he is going. Jesus says Peter can’t follow now but will later — a hint at Peter’s own future martyrdom.
Peter protests: why not now? He will lay down his life for Jesus!

f.w: I will lay down my life for thy sake

n: Jesus gently questions his confidence and foretells that before the rooster crows, Peter will deny him three times. Peter’s love is real; his strength is not yet.

f.w: The cock shall not crow, till thou hast denied me thrice
f.g: thrice = three times.
